Obviously hit up Roppongi on a Friday or Saturday night. If you're staying in Shibuya, it might be a bit tricky getting back to your place at 5am, so consider a hotel room in the area for the night. Go to Roppongi tower while you're there.

If you're staying in Shibuya, I also recommend stopping by Harajuku and the Meijii Shrine. Get some pictures with the cosplay girls in front of the shrine before you go in.

Eat Yakiniku (korean bbq). My favorite chain restaurant is GyuKaku, but if you know any locals they can probably recommend better.

March is when the Cherry Blossom festivals get going. Depending on when you go, there should be some good parties to be found in just about any big park in Tokyo. I recommend Yoyogi park, it has some EPIC cherry blossom parties. And Yaskuni shrine is nearby, check it out for the history and the beautiful cherry blossom trees.

Be careful if you go partying in Shinjuku, go in a group, and don't take any bank cards with you.

If you like anime, manga, or collectibles, check out the shop Madarake in Shibuya. You'll want the basement. Also, spend a day in Ikebukuro and go to Sunshine City. Check out J-World (a Jump themed attraction) and Namjatown (a Namco themed attraction). Eat the Gyoza (fried dumplings) at Namjatown.

Let's be honest here: No matter how much you improve the educational standards in any given society, you still end up with a sizeable share of people who will neither write a doctoral thesis on quantum physics, nor get the qualifications for some kind of office job. Now, this normally wouldn't be a problem in itself - society does need farmers, construction workers, factory workers, and so on. At the end of the day it's good, honest work that needs to be done. But as the field of robotics and AI becomes ever more sophisticated, many of these jobs will eventually be done by machine, netting a significant part of the population who can't get a job because a robot can do it without wages. And as the machines get even more advanced, even some type of office and accounting jobs will totally be relegated to computers.

How to you fix this issue? Even if we assume that we get a post-scarcity society where every citizen gets more than enough money to live each month, the lack of occupation would quickly lead to boredom, and boredom typically leads to trouble.
Mechanization and the fate of the working class

Machines are only taking the jobs which need little brainwork. This leaves it to the humans to do the jobs the machines can't. The industrialization didn't lower living standards on the longer term. More mechanization got us to a society with a much better living standard than before industrialization.

Not everyone needs to "write a doctoral thesis on quantum physics", there are lots of tasks humans do better then machines. And most of them can be learned be training. And that won't change soon.
